scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that the partner
network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) feels very slow -- they are sure the inter-AS peering
between router1 and router2 is congested and adding huge latency. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The inter-AS peering between router1 and router2 is healthy and not adding latency. End-to-end latency pc1→pc2 is ~1.1 ms with 0% loss (10/10 pings received), and reverse is ~1.0 ms. The BGP session is Established on both routers with prefixes exchanged (router1 and router2 “show ip bgp summary” each report 1 neighbor up, Up/Down ~00:02:31). On the peering interfaces (router1:eth0, router2:eth0) traffic-control stats show no drops/overlimits/backlog, and ethtool reports 10G full-duplex link detected on both sides. This rules out congestion on the inter-AS link.

iperf throughput is ~134–137 Mbit/s in both directions. We do see some TCP retransmissions that correlate with TX dropped counters on the pc2 LAN segment: router2:eth1 shows TX dropped 223, and pc2:eth0 shows TX dropped 339 (ip -s link). However, qdisc fq_codel on those ports reports zero drops, indicating occasional driver/virt-queue drops below the qdisc layer during bursty tests, not sustained congestion. These minor access-link drops do not manifest as high latency and are not on the inter-AS path the user suspects.

Root cause: No network fault on the inter-AS peering; the user’s “slow” perception is not due to router1–router2 congestion.

Corrective fix: No restart required. If desired, tune the pc2 access side (e.g., increase txqueuelen or check host load). Do not restart the routers; the peering is stable and clean.
